conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Patel from the surgery team. I understand you came in with abdominal pain. Can you tell me where it hurts most right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It started around my G-tube like usual, but now it’s more up here—epigastric and right upper side. It feels like when I had an ulcer before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Any vomiting, black stools, or blood when you spit up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No blood. No vomiting. I’m just nauseated and it hurts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have you been able to keep your tube feeds running?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continuous at about 40 mL an hour. No diarrhea. But it’s leaking around the tube a bit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. Any fevers, chills, chest pain, or shortness of breath?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: What have you taken for pain at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Tylenol, but it barely touched it. I ran out of oxycodone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Given your history of marginal ulcers after the Roux-en-Y, we want to be careful and avoid NSAIDs like ibuprofen or naproxen, and aspirin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know. I’m allergic anyway, and I’m scared to take anything that could make an ulcer worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. On exam your belly is soft, but you’re tender where you describe. Your G-tube site doesn’t look infected—no redness or swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why does it hurt so much? And why the right side?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right upper pain can come from the gallbladder, liver area, or stomach/ulcer pain that radiates. In the ED you had a right upper quadrant ultrasound, and it did not show gallstones or gallbladder infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not my gallbladder?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct—no evidence of cholecystitis or stones on the ultrasound. Your labs also don’t suggest pancreatitis; the lipase was normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Then you think it’s the ulcer again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s our leading concern—recurrence of a marginal ulcer. The plan is bowel rest for now, IV fluids, and strong acid suppression with IV pantoprazole. We’ll watch your symptoms closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Does that mean I can’t have anything by mouth?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For tonight, we’ll keep you on bowel rest except small sips of water if you’re not nauseated. We’ll continue your tube feeds as tolerated since you rely on them, and we’ll monitor your blood sugars.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried about hypoglycemia if feeds stop.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. We’ll keep the feeds running and adjust if needed. If you can’t tolerate them, we’ll support you with IV fluids and close glucose checks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the leaking around the tube? It’s messy and burns my skin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll have nursing help with dressing changes and skin protection. Since you already have revisional G-tube surgery scheduled, we’ll focus on keeping the site clean and watching for increased redness, pain, or drainage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can you move the surgery up? I’m so tired of coming back here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. I can’t promise we can move it sooner, but we’ll communicate with your surgeon’s office and make sure the plan is on track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m also really anxious. Every time it hurts like this I think something is tearing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. Right now your vital signs are stable, you’re not having bleeding symptoms, and your exam doesn’t show signs of a surgical emergency like guarding or rebound. We’ll keep reassessing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I get pain medicine? Tylenol isn’t enough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll use acetaminophen and can use opioid pain medication as needed while we treat the underlying irritation. We’ll aim to keep it safe and transition to oral-only as you improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Quick update: your blood work is overall reassuring. Your white count was a bit higher on one draw, but you’re afebrile and stable, so we’ll continue observation and ulcer treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about that lactate number they mentioned?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One lactate value was elevated, but another was normal earlier. Given your stable exam and vitals, we’re not seeing signs of poor blood flow to the gut. We’ll keep monitoring and repeat labs if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no surgery tonight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No surgery planned. This looks most consistent with ulcer-related pain, and we’re treating it medically.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How was the night? Any vomiting or worsening pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting. Pain is still there but not as sharp. The burning is a little better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s encouraging. We’re continuing the IV pantoprazole. Today we’re also adding sucralfate, which coats the ulcer area and helps it heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is sucralfate like an antacid?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Different—pantoprazole reduces acid production. Sucralfate forms a protective barrier over irritated lining. Together they often help symptoms improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I drink anything besides water?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For now, water by mouth only. Your nutrition will come through the G-tube feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m scared to go home and have it flare again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll make sure you have a clear plan: continue acid suppression at home and take sucralfate four times a day. And we’ll review warning signs that should bring you back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Midday check-in: how’s the pain after starting sucralfate?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s noticeably better. Still sore, but I’m not curled up anymore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Are you tolerating the tube feeds without nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Same rate. And I’ve been sipping water okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll keep the feeds running and continue the IV medication today. If you keep improving, we can switch you back to your home regimen by discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can you remind me what I should avoid so I don’t make the ulcer worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—avoid all NSAIDs and aspirin, and also avoid alcohol and tobacco. Those can worsen ulcers and delay healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t smoke or drink. I just want this to stop happening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know it’s exhausting. The revisional G-tube surgery you have scheduled should help address the tube-related issues. For the ulcer symptoms, staying consistent with the PPI and sucralfate is key.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You look more comfortable today. How’s the RUQ/epigastric pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. I still feel tender, but it’s manageable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. You’ve been stable—no fever, blood pressure and heart rate have been good, and you’re tolerating tube feeds and water. We’re planning discharge later today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What meds am I going home on? I don’t want to mess it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue your home medications, and specifically for this episode: lansoprazole 30 mg twice daily and sucralfate 1 gram four times daily. For pain: acetaminophen as needed, and a small supply of oxycodone liquid as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried about running out again and ending up back here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll prescribe it with no refills, but we’ll also emphasize using it only when needed and leaning on the ulcer treatment to prevent the pain from escalating. If pain is not controlled despite the plan, call your surgeon rather than waiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my tube feeds at home—same as before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: At discharge: water by mouth only, and NutriHep at 50 mL per hour continuously through the G-tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the leaking? When should I worry?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Monitor the site for increased redness, worsening pain, or drainage that’s foul-smelling or unusual in color. If you see that, or you develop fever over 101.5, severe abdominal pain, chest pain, shortness of breath, severe nausea/vomiting, bloating, or you can’t tolerate feeds or water—call your surgeon or come to the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I also take meds for anxiety and depression—those stay the same?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—continue your fluoxetine, aripiprazole, and lorazepam as prescribed, and zolpidem at night if needed. If anxiety spikes because of pain, let us know—sometimes adjusting the medical plan helps more than adding sedating meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before you go, any last questions about the diagnosis or why we treated it this way?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just to be clear—since the ultrasound was normal, you’re confident it wasn’t my gallbladder?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct. The ultrasound showed no stones and no signs of gallbladder inflammation. Your improvement with IV acid suppression and sucralfate also supports ulcer irritation as the cause.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. I’m nervous but relieved it’s better. I’ll stick to the meds and the tube feed plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the right approach. We’ll discharge you home now, and you’ll follow up with your surgeon as planned for the upcoming G-tube revision. Please don’t hesitate to call if symptoms return or worsen.
